subChunks.title: The Relational Model and Foreign Keys
subChunks.hookHtml: A single table can only take you so far. Real data lives across many tables — and the rules that connect them are the heart of the relational model.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem single tables create

Suppose you store a mentor's name in every apprentice row:

id | name   | mentor_name | mentor_specialty
 1 | Alice  | Aldric      | Evocation
 2 | Bjorn  | Sereth      | Divination
 3 | Cassia | Aldric      | Evocation

Aldric's name appears twice. Change his specialty and you must update two rows — miss one and the data is inconsistent. This is called update anomaly.

The relational solution

Split into two tables. Reference the mentor by a numeric ID:

mentors:     id | name   | specialty
              1 | Aldric | Evocation
              2 | Sereth | Divination

apprentices: id | name   | mentor_id
              1 | Alice  | 1
              2 | Bjorn  | 2
              3 | Cassia | 1

mentor_id in the apprentices table is a foreign key — it references the primary key of the mentors table.

Referential integrity

A foreign key constraint prevents you from: (a) inserting an apprentice with a mentor_id that does not exist in mentors, and (b) deleting a mentor who still has apprentices. The database enforces consistency automatically.

One-to-many vs many-to-many

  • One-to-many: one mentor has many apprentices — foreign key lives on the "many" side (apprentices.mentor_id)
  • Many-to-many: an apprentice can complete many quests; a quest can be completed by many apprentices — requires a junction table (quest_completions with apprentice_id and quest_id)

storyBeats.text: Cipher opens two side-by-side ledgers: Mentors and Apprentices. Each apprentice entry shows only a number where the mentor name used to be.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Aldric changed his specialty last year. If his name appeared in every apprentice row, I would have found forty inconsistent records. Instead I changed one row in the mentors ledger. The number — the foreign key — keeps them linked without duplicating the information.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Relational design analysis

Study the two-table design below. Answer: (1) what update anomaly does separating the tables prevent, (2) what would happen if you tried to insert an apprentice with mentor_id = 99 (which does not exist), and (3) identify the foreign key and which table's primary key it references.

mentors(id PK, name, specialty)
apprentices(id PK, name, rank, xp, mentor_id FK → mentors.id)
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Without the split, changing a mentor's specialty would require updating every apprentice row that references that mentor. A single table risks update anomalies — inconsistent data if any row is missed. Separating the tables means mentor data exists in exactly one place.

(2) A foreign key constraint would reject the INSERT — mentor_id = 99 references a row that does not exist in the mentors table. The database enforces referential integrity automatically.

(3) The foreign key is apprentices.mentor_id. It references mentors.id (the primary key of the mentors table). This is a one-to-many relationship: one mentor can appear in many apprentice rows.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Describe the junction table you would create to model this relationship: an apprentice can complete many quests; a quest can be completed by many apprentices. Name the table and its columns, identifying primary and foreign keys.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Junction table: quest_completions

Columns:
- id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (surrogate key for the completion event)
- apprentice_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES apprentices(id)
- quest_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES quests(id)
- completed_at TEXT (date/timestamp of completion)
- score INTEGER (score for this attempt)

This is a many-to-many relationship. Neither apprentices.id nor quests.id can be put in the other table directly — that would only model one-to-many. The junction table holds one row per (apprentice, quest) completion event.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why we split data into multiple tables, what a foreign key is, and what referential integrity means using the mentor/apprentice example.

options: When the same fact is stored in multiple rows and changing it requires updating all copies — missing one causes inconsistency
When an UPDATE statement fails due to a constraint violation
When two users update the same row simultaneously
When a column is updated to NULL accidentally
questions.answer: When the same fact is stored in multiple rows and changing it requires updating all copies — missing one causes inconsistency
questions.explanation: Update anomalies occur in denormalised tables where the same fact is duplicated across rows. The relational model solves this by storing each fact in exactly one place.

options: A column in one table that references the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity
A column that uniquely identifies each row in its own table
A column with a UNIQUE constraint
An index on a frequently queried column
questions.answer: A column in one table that references the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity
questions.explanation: A foreign key creates a link between tables. It must reference a value that exists in the referenced table's primary key column. The database rejects insertions or deletions that would break this link.

questions.prompt: In a one-to-many relationship between mentors (one) and apprentices (many), where does the foreign key live?
questions.explanation: The foreign key always lives on the 'many' side of a one-to-many relationship. Each apprentice row stores the id of its one mentor. The mentor table needs no reference back — it is the 'one' side.

questions.prompt: Why is a junction table required for a many-to-many relationship?
options: Because you cannot put a list of IDs in a single column — each relationship needs its own row in a separate table
Because many-to-many requires two foreign keys in the same table
Because primary keys must be unique across all tables
Because the many-to-many relationship requires a view, not a table
questions.answer: Because you cannot put a list of IDs in a single column — each relationship needs its own row in a separate table
questions.explanation: Relational databases store scalar values in cells — you cannot store an array. A many-to-many relationship (apprentice ↔ quest) is represented by one row per pairing in a junction table, with foreign keys to both parent tables.
